content.page_summary: Guidance on management of sleep-disordered breathing in heart failure (HF), recommendations about adaptive servo-ventilation and phrenic nerve stimulation, guidance on hyperlipidaemia/statin use in HF, and notes on hyperuricaemia/gout in chronic heart failure (CHF).

Sleep-disordered breathing.prevalence: Occurs in more than one third of patients with HF; even more prevalent in acute HF (AHF).
Sleep-disordered breathing.common_types: Central sleep apnoea (CSA), obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), and mixed pattern. CSA is most common in HFrEF; HFmrEF is the most common cause of CSA.
Sleep-disordered breathing.prognosis: CSA and OSA associated with worse prognosis in HF; OSA associated with increased risk of incident HF in men.

Investigation.history: History taking should involve partners; questionnaires useful to identify at-risk patients.
Investigation.diagnosis: Home monitoring can usually identify and distinguish type, but overnight polysomnography remains definitive.

Therapies and recommendations.adaptive_servo-ventilation: Not recommended in HFrEF with predominant CSA based on SERVE-HF results; neutral for composite primary endpoint but increased all-cause and CV mortality with adaptive servo-ventilation.
Therapies and recommendations.phrenic_nerve_stimulation: Transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation tested in a prospective multicentre randomized trial of 151 patients with CSA; primary efficacy endpoint (reduction in apnoea–hypopnoea index to 6 months) achieved, improved sleep quality and QOL, no difference in safety endpoints vs control; similar results in 96 patients with HF.
Therapies and recommendations.positive_pressure_airway_mask: Patients being considered for positive pressure treatment must undergo formal sleep study to document predominant type. When sleep-disordered breathing caused by OSA, nocturnal hypoxaemia can be treated with oxygen, CPAP, bi-level PAP and adaptive servo-ventilation, but none shown to improve HF outcomes. When caused by CSA, positive pressure masks are contraindicated in HFrEF patients; implantable phrenic nerve stimulation may be considered for symptomatic relief.

Hyperlipidaemia and lipid-modifying ther.evidence_summary: Two large RCTs (mainly HFrEF) and a meta-analysis of 24 RCTs showed no benefit of statin treatment on CV mortality or stroke in patients with HFrEF. Meta-analyses of CORONA and GISSI-HF showed reduction in HF hospitalizations and a small reduction in MI.
Hyperlipidaemia and lipid-modifying ther.recommendation: Routine administration of statins in patients with HF without other indications (e.g., CAD) is not recommended. No need to discontinue statins after occurrence of HF because no evidence of harm.

Gout and arthritis / Hyperuricaemia.prevalence: Hyperuricaemia common in patients with CHF with prevalence up to 50%.
Gout and arthritis / Hyperuricaemia.causes_and_consequences: May be caused or aggravated by diuretic treatment; related to symptoms, exercise capacity, severity of diastolic dysfunction and long-term prognosis.
Gout and arthritis / Hyperuricaemia.risk_association: For every 1 mg/dL increase in serum uric acid, risk of all-cause mortality and HF hospitalization increases by ~4% and ~28%, respectively.
Gout and arthritis / Hyperuricaemia.treatment: Both febuxostat and allopurinol reduce serum uric acid (implied benefit on urate levels).
